title: Tool annotations, output schemas and structured content
summary: Annotations are behaviour hints about a tool, `outputSchema` declares the shape of its result, and `structuredContent` carries machine-readable output next to the text the model reads.
useIf: Hosts need hints for approval UX, or downstream code needs typed results from a tool.
avoidIf: You would rely on annotations for security decisions about a server you do not control.

explain.md: **Annotations** describe how a tool behaves so a host can shape its approval UI. They are hints only, and clients MUST treat them as untrusted unless they come from trusted servers [[r6]] [[r37]]. Missing hints default to the cautious reading, shown below.

explain.caption: Annotation hints and their defaults
head: Hint
Default
Meaning
Safe host use
rows: The tool does not change its environment
Fewer prompts only for tools from reviewed servers
May delete or overwrite. Meaningful only when not read-only
Repeating a call with the same arguments has no extra effect
Reaches systems outside a closed domain, such as the web

explain.md: **Output schemas** came with structured tool output in 2025-06-18. A tool may declare `outputSchema`, a JSON Schema (2020-12 by default) for its result. It then returns `structuredContent` that conforms to the schema, and SHOULD also return the serialized JSON in a `TextContent` block so hosts that ignore structured output still work. Clients SHOULD validate results against the schema. In 2026-07-28 `structuredContent` may be any JSON value and schemas accept any 2020-12 keywords [[r1]].

explain.title: Not the same as LLM structured outputs
explain.md: MCP structured content is a result format for tool output. Model-side structured outputs constrain what a model generates. They solve different problems and can be used together.

Errors stay separate: an execution failure sets `isError: true` and the content explains why, so the model can adjust. Input validation errors count as execution errors, a change made in 2025-11-25 [[r31]].

whereToUse: Approval UIs that colour or batch confirmations by destructive and read-only hints
Tools whose results feed code or another tool, such as a price lookup returning numbers and currency
Typed clients that validate results before use
Retry logic that checks `idempotentHint` before replaying a call

use: The server is operated and reviewed by you
A downstream consumer needs a stable result shape
You want hosts to differentiate risky and safe tools in the UI
You need to validate output before passing it on
avoid: Granting trust to an unreviewed third-party server because its hints look safe
Using annotations as the only access control
Declaring an `outputSchema` you do not keep in sync with real results
flips: The server is third-party: ignore hints for policy and use an allow-list plus approvals
Hosts ignore structured content: keep the serialized JSON in a text block

pitfalls.symptom: A destructive tool ran without a prompt
pitfalls.cause: The host skipped approval because the server set `readOnlyHint: true`
pitfalls.fix: Base auto-approval on your own allow-list and review, not on server-supplied hints

pitfalls.symptom: Clients reject a result or silently drop structured data
pitfalls.fix: Validate on the server in tests and keep the schema versioned with the tool

pitfalls.symptom: An older host shows an empty result
pitfalls.cause: Only `structuredContent` was returned and the host reads `content`
pitfalls.fix: Also return the serialized JSON in a `TextContent` block

scenarios.title: Cutting approval prompts for a third-party server
scenarios.situation: Users are tired of approval prompts. A vendor's server marks most tools `readOnlyHint: true`. The host owner wants to skip prompts for those tools.
unknowns: Has security reviewed this server and its tool list?
Are tool definitions pinned or can they change?
scenarios.question: How do you reduce prompts safely?

options.name: Review the server, allow-list specific tools, then skip prompts only for those
options.why: Your own review and pinning carry the trust. Hints can still inform the UI.
options.tradeoff: Upfront review work and re-review when definitions change.

options.name: Keep prompting for every call
options.tradeoff: Approval fatigue pushes users to click through everything.

options.name: Skip prompts for every tool that sets `readOnlyHint: true`
options.why: Annotations from an untrusted server are only claims, and a rug pull can flip them.
options.tradeoff: Acceptable for a server you build and operate yourself.

flips.if: The server is internal, reviewed and version-pinned
Tools also read untrusted web content
flips.then: Keep confirmations, since `openWorldHint` signals injection exposure.

scenarios.takeaway: Trust comes from review, not from labels.

scenarios.title: Typed results for a pricing pipeline
scenarios.situation: A `get_price` tool feeds a pricing calculation in code and is also read by the model. Several host versions are in use, some older.
unknowns: How often does the result shape change?
scenarios.question: How should the tool return its result?

options.name: Declare `outputSchema`, return `structuredContent` and the same JSON as text
options.why: Typed consumers validate the structure and older hosts still read the text block.
options.tradeoff: Duplicate payload bytes and a schema to maintain.

options.name: Return free text and parse it with regular expressions
options.why: Parsing breaks when wording changes and cannot be validated.
options.tradeoff: Fine for a prototype with a human reader only.

options.name: Return `structuredContent` without text
options.tradeoff: Hosts that ignore structured output see an empty result.

flips.if: Every consumer is your own and current
flips.then: You may drop the duplicate text.
Version the tool name or schema to avoid breaking consumers.

scenarios.takeaway: Use schemas for code consumers and keep a text fallback for compatibility.

quiz.q: A tool carries no annotations. How should a host read its behaviour?
options: Not read-only, destructive, not idempotent and open-world
Destructive only if the name says so
quiz.explain: The defaults are cautious: `readOnlyHint` false, `destructiveHint` true, `idempotentHint` false and `openWorldHint` true. Assuming safety when hints are absent is the mistake.

quiz.q: A host auto-approves tools whose server sets `readOnlyHint: true`. What is the core flaw?
options: Hints are untrusted unless the server is trusted
`readOnlyHint` is not defined in the spec
quiz.explain: Clients MUST treat annotations as untrusted unless they come from trusted servers, so a malicious or changed server can lie. The hint exists in the spec, schemas are unrelated and TLS does not decide approvals.

flashcards.front: What are the default annotation values?
flashcards.back: `readOnlyHint` false, `destructiveHint` true, `idempotentHint` false and `openWorldHint` true. They are hints, not guarantees.

flashcards.front: Why also return text next to `structuredContent`?
flashcards.back: A tool SHOULD include the serialized JSON in a `TextContent` block for hosts that ignore structured output.

flashcards.front: Is MCP structured content the same as model structured outputs?
flashcards.back: No. It is a tool result format. Model structured outputs constrain generation. They are unrelated and can be combined.
